chunk_findings.detail: The parent serializes `called_from` through `str()`, which is lossy for the None case. `serve(repo, ...)` declares `called_from: Path | None = None` and passes that value straight to `Server(repo, called_from=called_from)`, so `srv.called_from` can legitimately be None; `_offload` then writes `"called_from": "None"` into the job and `_worker_main` reconstructs it as `Path("None")` — a *relative, non-existent* path — instead of None. Demonstrated input: start the server via `serve(repo)` (no `called_from`), then call any tool in `OFFLOADED`, e.g. `ddflow_review`. The same request handled inline (offload disabled, or a non-offloaded tool) constructs its `Server` with `called_from=None`, but the offloaded run constructs it with `Path("None")`. Any behaviour keyed on `called_from` (caller-directory/repo resolution, attribution recorded in the event log) therefore differs between the two paths, and a `Server` that does anything filesystem-ish with the value (`resolve()`, `is_dir()`, repo discovery) will operate on a bogus directory or fail outright, turning every offloaded call into a "worker process ended … without an answer" reply.

chunk_findings.detail: The predicate classifies untrusted client input but assumes `params["name"]` is hashable. `params.get("name") in OFFLOADED` performs a set membership test, which hashes the operand; a `tools/call` request whose `name` is a JSON array or object raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` (or `'dict'`). chunk_findings.detail: The changed loop replaces the single-threaded `outp.write(...)+outp.flush()` with `notify(...)`, but `notify` is now invoked concurrently from several places: the reader thread (parse-error path at the `except json.JSONDecodeError` branch and the inline `if reply is not None: notify(reply)` path) and every relay thread spawned by `_offload(srv, msg, notify)` for an offloaded request. Before this diff, `outp` only ever had one writer; now a relay thread's reply and a main-thread reply/parse-error can be emitted at the same time. If `notify` is the same write-then-flush helper the diff just replaced (`json.dumps(m) + "\n"` then `outp.write`/`outp.flush`), the two calls interleave on the buffered stream: one thread's flush can push a half-written line, or the two JSON objects can share a line. Concrete input: over stdio, the client pipelines request `A` (a `tools/call` that `_offloaded` matches, so it is handed to `_offload`) and request `B` (anything not offloaded); `A` completes in its relay thread at almost the same moment the reader thread emits `notify(reply_B)`, so the client receives a corrupted JSON-RPC frame it cannot parse, and — matching the reported symptom — the session's tool list is not restored. The same concurrency applies to `srv.handle` running on the reader thread for `B` while the relay thread for `A` is still inside the handler, mutating whatever shared server state `srv` keeps.

chunk_findings.detail: `_frames` registers the *file descriptor* of `proc.stdout` with a selector but then drains it with a buffered `proc.stdout.readline()`. `subprocess` was started with `text=True, bufsize=1`, so `readline()` ultimately issues a single raw read on the pipe (TextIOWrapper.readline reads through `read1` into the 8 KiB `BufferedReader`), which returns *all* bytes currently available. If two replies are coalesced into that one read, the second line stays in the Python-level buffer while the kernel pipe is empty; the next `sel.select(left)` therefore blocks until the deadline even though the frame was already received, and the loop exits with the id still in `want`. Concretely, in `test_a_long_call_does_not_hold_up_the_calls_behind_it` the client sends `ping` (id 3) and `tools/call ddflow_status` (id 4) back to back; if the server's two writes land before the client is rescheduled after its first `readline()`, `order` is `[3]`, line 66's `assert 3 in order and 4 in order` fails with "the calls behind a long one were not answered while it ran" — even though the server answered both. The same coalescing makes `after = {f["id"]: f for f in _frames(proc, {3, 4})}` in the second test intermittently miss id 4 and trip `set(after) == {3, 4}` on correct code. The fix is to read from the already-buffered stream (e.g. check `proc.stdout` for a pending line before/alongside `select`, or use an unbuffered raw reader) so the harness cannot lose data that Python has already pulled out of the pipe.

chunk_findings.detail: `_offload` serialises the connection's location as `str(srv.called_from)` and `_worker_main` reconstructs it unconditionally with `Path(job["called_from"])`. `serve()` declares `called_from: Path | None = None`, and the real stdio path enables offload precisely when the caller passes no streams (`offload = stdin is None`), which is orthogonal to `called_from`. So the combination `serve(repo)` (or any caller that leaves `called_from` at its default while offload is on) makes `srv.called_from` `None`, `str(None)` produces the literal `"None"`, and the worker's `Server` is built with `called_from=Path("None")` instead of `None`. That value is truthy and points at a directory named `None` (resolved relative to the worker's cwd), so any offloaded tool that branches on `called_from` — e.g. `if srv.called_from: …` to locate the invoking project — takes the "caller supplied a path" branch and resolves against a bogus location, while the in-process path (`offload=False`, e.g. a caller supplying its own streams) correctly sees `None`. The asymmetry is visible in isolation: `None` is intentionally representable in `serve`, but the job/worker round-trip drops that representation, so the two code paths disagree for the same session.

`LAUNCHERS` includes interactive shells (`bash`, `zsh`, `sh`, `dash`), but those are not "processes that only start another" — the harness itself (or the process whose child shells carry the identity) is frequently a shell. chunk_findings.detail: `declare` writes `agent` verbatim to the record file (`f.write_text(agent + "\n")`) without validating it against `_NAME`, yet the reader `declared` only returns a record whose content full-matches `_NAME` (`[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}`), otherwise it skips the file and keeps climbing to another ancestor. So `declare` can return `""` ("recorded") for a value the shell will never see — the exact "silently back" split the module exists to prevent, and which its own docstring says `declare` must report: "Returns \"\" when it did, else why not -- which ddflow_identify reports, because a declaration the shell will not see is the original split, silently back." This diff does not fix the bug it claims to fix. The only functional change on the identity path is a name-validation guard in `harness_identity.declare`; the `mcp.py` hunk merely re-words the advisory string. Neither the shell's identity resolution nor `harness_identity.declared`'s read path is touched, so a `ddflow_identify` performed on the MCP connection still writes a record keyed to a process the shell CLI is not descended from, and the shell still falls back to its own tree-derived name.

Concretely, replaying the probe given in the intent against this patch: `ddflow_identify` as `kilo-onboard` over MCP, then `ddflow claim B-onboard-harness` executed through the shell — `claim` still resolves the lease holder via the shell's tree derivation (e.g. `Monster3-ddflow-7267fe`), because no code added here makes it consult the MCP-written record. `ddflow_heartbeat` on the MCP connection therefore still answers "no lease held B-onboard-harness", i.e. the single agent's claim and heartbeat remain split across two identities, exactly the reported symptom.

Worse, the newly added `test_a_record_for_a_process_that_is_not_an_ancestor_is_ignored` asserts `H.declared(repo) == ""` for a record written by a non-ancestor process — which is precisely the mechanism that produces the split (the MCP server is not an ancestor of the user's shell). So the change codifies the root-cause behavior as intended while leaving the bug open. The other added test (`test_an_unusable_name_is_reported_not_recorded`) only exercises the new guard; it would fail before the patch, but it is unrelated to `ddflow_identify` reaching the shell.

chunk_findings.detail: `_stat` reads `/proc/<pid>/stat` with `Path.read_text()`, which decodes using the locale encoding under `errors="strict"`, and the only handler around it is `except OSError`. A process `comm` (field 2 of the stat line) can hold bytes that are not valid in that encoding: the kernel copies up to 15 bytes into `comm`, so a non-ASCII executable/PR_SET_NAME value longer than 15 bytes is truncated mid-multibyte-character and becomes an invalid sequence; `prctl(PR_SET_NAME)` can also inject arbitrary bytes. `UnicodeDecodeError` is a subclass of `ValueError`, not `OSError`, so it is not caught: if any ancestor of the CLI has such a `comm` (e.g. the harness itself), `declared()` propagates the exception instead of returning the declared name (or `""`), and `declare()` — whose contract explicitly says "Never raises" — raises out of `_harness`/`_stat`. The same strict-decode pattern is used in `_dir` for the `.git` file and `commondir` contents (a repo path with non-ASCII bytes under a POSIX/C locale), which likewise raises out of `declare`/`declared`/`own`. The fix is to read bytes (or pass `errors="replace"`), as `_wrapper_shell` already does for `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`. Note this is worse than the original symptom: rather than resolving to the wrong identity, the CLI's identity resolution now fails with an uncaught exception.

chunk_findings.detail: The declaration is keyed only by the repo: both the write (`harness_identity.declare(self.repo, want)` in `mcp.py`) and the read (`harness_identity.declared(self.repo)` here) pass nothing but `self.repo`, so the record is a single shared slot rather than a per-agent/per-connection one. Consider the very configuration the new MCP message in this diff calls out ("Every agent in this tree derives the SAME name, so if you are one of several here, declare one"): agent A's MCP connection calls `ddflow_identify A` (record = "A"), then agent B's connection calls `ddflow_identify B` (record = "B", overwriting A). A shell command from A — which by the whole point of this change no longer derives its own name but reads `declared(repo)` — resolves to "B", so `ddflow claim B-onboard-harness` records the lease under B. A's own heartbeart/job_run still carries `self.agent == "A"` (set on its connection and re-adopted from `harness_identity.own(self.repo)` at server start), so it answers "no lease held" / "held by B, not you". That is exactly the Bfad021e8d9 split resurfaces: MCP identity and shell identity diverge again, now driven by whichever connection declared last rather than by tree derivation. The concurrent use of `harness_identity.own` (MCP server init) versus `harness_identity.declared` (CLI) does not help, because a cross-process slot the shell can read cannot be scoped to the declaring connection; any repo/tree shared by two agents (the case the code's own advice presumes, and the multi-worktree case in the bug report) makes `ddflow claim`/`ddflow_heartbeat`/`ddflow_job_run` attribute work to the wrong agent.
